notes.meaning: The people pray for their king as he prepares to go to war. They ask the Lord to hear the king's private prayers and keep him safe from harm. Calling God the God of Jacob reminds them of how God protected Jacob whenever he was in distress.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note the Hebrew verbs can be read as confident statements that the Lord will answer, rather than as wishes.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church teaching often saw the speaker here addressing Christ directly as He enters His suffering on the cross.

notes.meaning: The people ask God to send help from His holy dwelling place. In David's day, this was the sacred tent in Jerusalem where the ark of the covenant sat. True strength does not come from ordinary human power, but from God's holy presence.

Before going into battle, the king presented offerings to ask for God's mercy and help. The people pray that God will look favorably on these gifts and accept them. An offering was a sacrifice burned on an altar to show devotion and seek peace with God.

The people ask God to bless the king's plans for defending the nation. Because David wanted what God wanted, his followers could pray with confidence for his success. When our plans line up with God's good purposes, we can trust Him to guide our steps.

The people are so sure of God's help that they plan to celebrate the victory before the fighting even begins. Raising a banner means lifting a military flag to give God all the credit for saving them. They end their chant by asking God to grant every single request the king made.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars propose translating the phrase for raising a banner as a verb meaning to rejoice or look with triumph.

notes.meaning: A single voice, likely the king or a priest, speaks with absolute confidence that God has heard the prayers. God's anointed refers to the king chosen by God and consecrated with holy oil, pointing ahead to the Messiah. By faith, the speaker treats the victory from heaven as something already accomplished.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine interpreted this verse as a prophecy of the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think this sudden change to confident certainty happened because a priest or prophet delivered an oracle of salvation during the service.

notes.meaning: Enemy nations bragged about their powerful war chariots and well-trained cavalry. God had forbidden Israel's kings from relying on large stables of horses, so God's people placed their trust in Him alone. Trusting in the Lord's name means relying completely on His power and faithfulness.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine treated chariots and horses as symbols of worldly wealth and the empty honors of earthly rulers.

notes.meaning: Armies that trust in military machines and earthly strength end up stumbling and falling to the ground. In contrast, God's people rise above their fears and stand strong on the battlefield. True stability comes from depending on God rather than earthly power.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine explained those who fell as ancient Israel stumbling in unbelief, while the Gentiles are raised up and stand firm through faith in Christ.

notes.meaning: The whole congregation closes the song with a united cry for help. They ask the Lord to save their king so that he can lead and protect the people. Even after expressing great confidence, God's people still end by asking Him to answer whenever they call.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars and ancient Greek and Latin translations divide the verse to say, Lord, save the king, and hear us when we call, taking the king as the earthly ruler rather than addressing God as the King.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine took the King to mean Christ in heaven, who hears our prayers and presents them before the Father.
